\title{A Deterministic Sampling Schedule for Multi-Scale Localised Network Centrality}
\author{%

\begin{abstract}
  Urban analysts measure the importance of streets by computing \emph{localised network centrality}: closeness and betweenness scores within distance thresholds. At metropolitan scales these computations become prohibitively expensive, and sampling is the natural remedy. However, when centrality patterns are compared across cities, sampling must be deterministic and network-agnostic; otherwise, different networks would carry different noise levels, making comparison meaningless.

  We present a sampling schedule that depends only on the analysis distance. The key insight is that, under localisation, the relevant population is not the entire network but the \emph{catchment} reachable within the distance threshold. Adapting the Eppstein--Wang bound to this local setting, and using a fixed canonical grid model to convert distance to catchment size, yields a simple formula for the fraction of nodes to sample at each distance, governed by a single error tolerance $\varepsilon$. The same sample serves both closeness and betweenness. We calibrate $\varepsilon$ directly on real networks: it is tuned so that the sparsest --- a low-density US suburb (Cary, NC) --- preserves node rankings, after which denser networks clear the target comfortably. Validation on three street networks spanning the density range (Greater London, \glaNnodes{} nodes; Greater Madrid, \madridNnodes{} nodes; Cary, \caryNnodes{} nodes) at 1--20\,km confirms that sampled rankings closely match exact rankings (Spearman $\rho \geq \overallMinRho$). The schedule is implemented in the open-source \cityseer{} Python package \citep{Simons2022}.
\end{abstract}

\textbf{Keywords:} network centrality, sampling, urban morphology, betweenness, harmonic closeness, computational efficiency

%==============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
%==============================================================================

Urban morphological analysis relies on localised network centrality to reveal patterns of accessibility and flow in street networks \citep{Cooper2015}. Two measures are central to this work: \emph{closeness} (how easily a node can reach its neighbours) and \emph{betweenness} (how often a node lies on shortest paths between others). Both are computed within distance thresholds that range from pedestrian ($\approx$500\,m) to metropolitan ($\approx$20\,km) scales, as implemented in tools such as sDNA \citep{Cooper2018} and \cityseer{} \citep{Simons2022}.

Exact computation requires running a shortest-path traversal from every node; the cost scales with both the number of nodes and the size of each node's neighbourhood. A multi-scale analysis of the Greater London network (\glaNnodes{} nodes) across ten distance thresholds takes several hours on a single core. Sampling offers a natural way to reduce this cost: instead of traversing from every node, traverse from a randomly selected fraction and scale up the result.

The challenge is comparability. Each node's centrality is computed over its own local neighbourhood, and these vary in size and density both within and across cities. If the sampling rate tracked local structure, nodes in dense and sparse areas would carry different noise levels, distorting comparisons within a city and --- the same argument applied across networks \citep{Strano2013} --- between cities. The schedule must therefore be \emph{deterministic} (the same distance always yields the same probability) and \emph{network-agnostic} (no dependence on local or global structure); existing adaptive methods such as KADABRA \citep{Borassi2019} produce network-dependent sample counts, precluding direct comparison.

The key quantity is \emph{reach}: the number of nodes reachable within the distance threshold. At short distances, reach is small and traversals are cheap, so sampling offers little benefit. At long distances, reach is large and each traversal updates many nodes at once, so both the potential speedup and the effective sample size grow with distance.

\citet{Eppstein2004} showed how to bound the required number of samples for global closeness using Hoeffding's concentration inequality. Their bound depends on the total number of nodes in the network. Our approach adapts this bound to the localised setting: under a distance threshold, only the nodes within that threshold matter, so we replace the global node count with the local reach. A canonical grid model then converts distance to reach, making the schedule depend on distance alone. Because each traversal naturally computes both closeness and betweenness, a single schedule serves both metrics.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A deterministic, network-agnostic sampling schedule for localised closeness and betweenness, where the sampling probability depends only on the analysis distance, with a single tolerance parameter $\varepsilon$ calibrated on the sparsest validated network.
  \item Empirical validation on three street networks spanning the urban density range --- Greater London (\glaNnodes{} nodes), Greater Madrid (\madridNnodes{} nodes), and the low-density suburb of Cary, NC (\caryNnodes{} nodes) --- at 1--20\,km, confirming that sampled rankings closely preserve exact rankings (Spearman $\rho \geq \overallMinRho$) for both metrics.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries} defines the centrality measures. Section~\ref{sec:models} derives the sampling model. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work. Sections~\ref{sec:setup}--\ref{sec:validation} describe the experiments and results. Sections~\ref{sec:discussion} and~\ref{sec:conclusion} discuss practical implications and conclude.

%==============================================================================
\section{Preliminaries}
\label{sec:preliminaries}
%==============================================================================

Both centrality measures are computed with a distance cutoff $d_{\max}$. We write $d$ for $d_{\max}$ when the context is clear.

\paragraph{Harmonic closeness.}
Closeness measures how easily a node can reach its surroundings \citep{Freeman1979}. We adopt the \emph{harmonic} form --- a sum of inverse distances over reachable nodes --- rather than classic closeness (the reciprocal of summed distances), because a distance threshold leaves most of the network unreachable, and classic closeness is ill-defined or unstable on the resulting disconnected, variably sized catchments. Harmonic closeness instead sums bounded per-node contributions, with unreachable nodes contributing zero, so it stays well-defined and comparable across catchments of different size while expressing the same intention \citep{Rochat2009, Boldi2014}. (This additive form is also what lets a single source's contribution be estimated independently under sampling; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_ht}.) For each node $v$ it sums the inverse distances to all nodes within the threshold, so nearby nodes contribute more than distant ones:
\begin{equation}
  C_H(v;\, d_{\max}) = \sum_{\substack{u \neq v \\ d(v,u) \leq d_{\max}}} \frac{1}{d(v, u)}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Betweenness.}
Betweenness measures how often a node acts as an intermediary \citep{Freeman1977}. For each node $v$, it counts the fraction of shortest paths (between all other pairs) that pass through $v$:
\begin{equation}
  C_B(v;\, d_{\max}) = \sum_{\substack{s \neq t,\; s \neq v,\; t \neq v \\ d(s,t) \leq d_{\max}}} \frac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}}
\end{equation}
where $\sigma_{st}$ is the total number of shortest paths from $s$ to $t$, and $\sigma_{st}(v)$ is the number that pass through $v$. Because shortest paths have optimal substructure, a distance-bounded traversal from each source discovers every node that could contribute to betweenness at that threshold. This property holds for shortest-path (metric) distance; angular (simplest-path) distance \citep{Turner2007} does not satisfy it in general (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).

\paragraph{Reach.}
The \emph{reach} of a node $v$ at threshold $d$ is simply the number of other nodes within distance $d$: $r_v = |\{u : d(v,u) \leq d\}|$. The mean reach across a network, $\bar{r}$, grows with the square of the distance. On a regular grid with inter-node spacing $s = \gridSpacing\,$m, reach follows $r_c = \pi d^2 / s^2$, ranging from about 100 nodes at 1\,km to over 40{,}000 at 20\,km. We call this the \emph{canonical reach} and use it later to build a network-agnostic sampling schedule.

\paragraph{Accuracy metric.}
We evaluate sampling quality using Spearman rank correlation ($\rho$) between sampled and exact centrality values. Urban applications rely on relative rankings (e.g., identifying the most central streets) rather than absolute values, so $\rho$ captures the quantity of practical interest.

%==============================================================================
\section{Sampling Model}
\label{sec:models}
%==============================================================================

\subsection{How many samples are enough?}

The approach follows \citet{Eppstein2004}: select a random subset of nodes as sources, run a distance-bounded shortest-path traversal from each, and scale up the result to estimate what the full computation would have produced (using inverse-probability weighting; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_ht}).

The question is how large the sample needs to be. Hoeffding's inequality \citep{Hoeffding1963} bounds the probability that a sample mean deviates from the true mean by more than a chosen tolerance $\varepsilon$. Applied to closeness estimation for a single target node $v$, it gives:
\[
  \Pr\!\left[\left|\hat{C}_H(v) - C_H(v)\right| > \varepsilon \cdot C_{\max}\right] \leq 2 \exp(-2k\varepsilon^2)
\]
where $k$ is the number of sampled sources that reach $v$, and $C_{\max}$ is the maximum possible contribution from a single source. To guarantee this for all nodes simultaneously, a union bound is applied.

In the global (unbounded) setting of \citet{Eppstein2004}, this union bound runs over all $n$ nodes in the network. Under localisation, however, only the nodes within $d_{\max}$ of $v$ can contribute to $v$'s estimate. This is the key simplification: the relevant population is the local neighbourhood of size $r$ (the reach), not the entire network of size $n$. The union bound therefore runs over $r$ rather than $n$ targets, and the required sample count scales with $\log r$ rather than $\log n$.

Replacing the network-specific reach with the canonical reach $r_c$ (Section~\ref{sec:canonical}) gives the required number of samples and the corresponding sampling probability:
\begin{equation}
  k = \frac{\log(2r_c/\delta)}{2\varepsilon^2}, \qquad
  p = \min\!\left(1,\; \frac{k}{r_c}\right)
  \label{eq:hoeffding_k}
\end{equation}

In words: $p$ is the fraction of nodes to sample at a given distance. It depends on two user-chosen parameters, $\varepsilon$ (error tolerance) and $\delta$ (failure probability), and on the canonical reach $r_c$, which is determined by the analysis distance alone. The \emph{functional form} $p(d) \propto \log(r_c)/r_c$ is fixed by the bound rather than fitted, and the grid spacing $s$ that sets $r_c$ is held at a fixed canonical value (Section~\ref{sec:canonical}). The schedule therefore has a single free parameter, the tolerance $\varepsilon$. We calibrate it once, on the sparsest validated network, to meet the rank-preservation target (Section~\ref{sec:validation}); the resulting default $\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$ then applies unchanged to every network.

At short distances the required sample count exceeds the number of reachable nodes, so $p = 1$ and computation is exact; as distance grows, $p$ falls and the speedup rises. How a network's actual reach compares to $r_c$ --- and the resulting over- or under-sampling --- is taken up with the grid model below (Section~\ref{sec:canonical}). Empirically, closeness error stays well within tolerance; betweenness, whose additive bound is far looser, is judged by rank preservation rather than by the bound (Section~\ref{sec:validation}).

\subsection{Shared computation for betweenness}

Each source traversal already explores the local neighbourhood via a bounded Dijkstra, from which betweenness follows by Brandes' backpropagation \citep{Brandes2001} at modest extra cost. We apply the same schedule to betweenness as a computational choice: the shared traversal makes it effectively free, and a metric-specific schedule would forfeit that saving. This is not entailed by the closeness bound --- a single source's betweenness credit can grow with reach rather than being bounded by a constant, and its contributions are heavier-tailed --- so the adequacy of one schedule for both metrics is established empirically (Section~\ref{sec:validation}), not by the bound.

\subsection{From reach to distance: the canonical grid model}
\label{sec:canonical}

The sampling probability $p$ depends on reach, which varies not only across networks but across nodes within the same network (dense cores have higher reach than sparse peripheries). To make $p$ depend on distance alone, we substitute a single conservative reference point: the reach of a regular grid with inter-node spacing $s$. On such a grid, the number of nodes within distance $d$ is simply the area of a circle divided by the area per node:
\begin{equation}
  r_c = \frac{\pi d^2}{s^2}
  \label{eq:canonical_reach}
\end{equation}
We set $s = \gridSpacing$\,m, a deliberately conservative (large) reference: it sits above typical mean street-segment lengths in European cities (city means $\approx$95--122\,m; \citealp{Strano2013}), so the canonical model under-counts reach for most networks. Holding $s$ fixed is what makes the schedule network-agnostic: the same distance yields the same $p$ everywhere, which is precisely what makes cross-network comparison valid. For dense networks, real reach exceeds the canonical estimate, so the schedule oversamples and the guarantee only strengthens. For the sparsest networks, real reach falls \emph{below} the canonical estimate (Figure~\ref{fig:val_reach}); there the grid model is no longer conservative, and it is the tolerance $\varepsilon$ --- calibrated on exactly such a network (Section~\ref{sec:validation}) --- that secures rank preservation. The trade-off is intentional: a small loss of potential speedup on dense networks buys a single, consistent sampling rate across all nodes and all networks at a given distance.

The resulting sampling probabilities at standard analysis distances are shown later in Table~\ref{tab:distance_lookup}.

\subsection{Algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
  \caption{Deterministic per-distance sampling for localised network centrality}
  \label{alg:deterministic}
  \begin{algorithmic}[1]
    \Require Network $G = (V, E)$ with live nodes $V_L \subseteq V$ and buffer nodes $V_B = V \setminus V_L$
    \Require Distance thresholds $D = \{d_1, \ldots, d_m\}$
    \Require Error tolerance $\varepsilon$ (default $\hoeffdingEpsilon$), failure probability $\delta$ (default $\hoeffdingDelta$)
    \Require Canonical grid spacing $s$ (default $\gridSpacing$\,m)
    \Ensure Closeness estimates $\hat{C}_H[d]$ and betweenness estimates $\hat{C}_B[d]$ for each $d \in D$

    \State $\varphi \gets |V_L| / |V|$ \Comment{Live fraction}
    \For{each distance $d \in D$}
    \State Compute canonical reach: $r_c \gets \pi d^2 / s^2$ \Comment{Eq.~\ref{eq:canonical_reach}}
    \State Compute required sources: $k \gets \ln(2r_c/\delta) / (2\varepsilon^2)$
    \State Compute sampling probability: $p \gets \min(1, k / r_c)$
    \If{$p \geq \varphi$} \Comment{Exact mode is cheaper; Section~\ref{sec:buffer}}
    \State Run exact computation (closeness sources $V_L$; betweenness sources $V$)
    \Else
    \State Sample sources $S \subseteq V$ by including each node independently with prob.\ $p$
    \For{each source $s \in S$} \Comment{$S$ includes both live and buffer nodes}
    \State Run distance-bounded Dijkstra from $s$
    \State Accumulate closeness to each live target $v$ via $1/(p \cdot d(s,v))$ \Comment{IPW}
    \State Run Brandes backpropagation; accumulate betweenness for live targets
    \EndFor
    \EndIf
    \EndFor

    \State \Return $\{\hat{C}_H[d],\, \hat{C}_B[d] : d \in D\}$
  \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

Each distance threshold draws an independent source set. In the implementation, distances where $p \geq \varphi$ (exact mode; see below) are batched so that a single Dijkstra per source serves all such distances simultaneously. Each sampled distance ($p < \varphi$) requires its own pass.

\subsection{Handling boundary effects}
\label{sec:buffer}

Nodes near the edge of a network have artificially low centrality because their neighbourhoods are truncated. The standard remedy \citep{Gil2017} is to surround the study area with a ring of \emph{buffer nodes}: paths can pass through them, but their own centrality values are not reported. Only the interior (\emph{live}) nodes receive results.

The two metrics treat buffer sources differently. \emph{Closeness} aggregates at the source, so in exact mode only live nodes need to run --- each gathers its own neighbourhood, buffer nodes included as destinations. Under sampling it aggregates at the target with inverse-probability weighting, and buffer nodes must be eligible sources or boundary live nodes lose the contributions they would receive from the buffer side --- \emph{edge roll-off}. \emph{Betweenness} runs from every node in both modes: a shortest path between two buffer nodes can pass through, and must credit, a live interior node, so restricting sources to live nodes would itself cause roll-off. Either way, the source pool includes buffer nodes.

This has a cost, and it differs by metric because exact mode runs a different number of sources for each. \emph{Closeness} exact mode traverses only the $n_L$ live sources, so sampling --- which must include the full $n$ sources, buffer included --- is faster only when
\begin{equation}
  p < \varphi \equiv \frac{n_L}{n},
  \label{eq:break_even}
\end{equation}
with effective speedup $\varphi / p$; for a network spanning $L$\,km with a $d_{\max}$\,km buffer on each side, $\varphi \approx (1 - 2d_{\max}/L)^2$. \emph{Betweenness} runs from every node even in exact mode (above), so its exact cost is already $n$ traversals and sampling is faster whenever $p < 1$, with speedup $1/p$. A combined closeness--betweenness call is gated by the closeness condition $p \geq \varphi$. When it triggers, the implementation falls back to exact mode, which produces identical (deterministic) results. This fallback is a cost optimisation, not part of the schedule: $p(d)$ remains deterministic and network-agnostic regardless.

\label{sec:related}

  \vspace{0.3em}
  \footnotesize \textsuperscript{*}Union bound over the $r$ nodes within each distance neighbourhood, not over all $n$ nodes globally (Section~\ref{sec:models}).

\emph{Source-sampling} selects a subset of nodes and traverses the network from each. \citet{Brandes2007} established this approach empirically for both closeness and betweenness. \citet{Geisberger2008} refined betweenness estimation with distance-weighted corrections. \citet{Bader2007} used adaptive sampling with per-vertex guarantees. None of these methods provides a deterministic, distance-based schedule suitable for comparative multi-scale analysis.

\emph{Path-sampling} \citep{Riondato2016, Borassi2019, Pellegrina2023} draws random source--target pairs and computes one shortest path per sample. It does not adapt easily to localised analysis: the set of admissible pairs depends on local morphology, each sample updates only one path (whereas a single source traversal updates all reachable nodes), and path-sampling applies only to betweenness. Our approach uses source-sampling, which naturally serves both metrics from the same traversals.

%==============================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}
%==============================================================================

Each network is analysed with a boundary buffer of depth equal to the maximum analysis distance (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}).

\paragraph{Validation networks.}
We validate on three real-world street networks spanning the urban density range, each built from official open road-network data. \emph{Greater London} (Ordnance Survey Open Roads; \glaNnodes{} live nodes) and \emph{Greater Madrid} (the official \emph{Red Viaria} road network; \madridNnodes{} live nodes) are dense metropolitan networks. \emph{Cary, NC} (US Census TIGER/Line; \caryNnodes{} live nodes) is a low-density planned suburb in the Raleigh region, with mean node degree $\approx 2.5$ --- markedly sparser than the metros and the real-world counterpart of low-connectivity suburban development. Each network is analysed within a \glaBuffer{}\,km buffer (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}); in every case the live study area is delimited by the administrative boundary geocoded from OpenStreetMap via OSMnx \citep{Boeing2017}, independently of the road-geometry source. We report the mean over three random seeds (inter-seed standard deviation in $\rho < 0.002$ at all distances). Ground truth uses all sources ($p = 1.0$) and is deterministic.

%==============================================================================
\section{Validation}
\label{sec:validation}
%==============================================================================

\subsection{Calibrating the tolerance}
\label{sec:calibration}

The schedule has a single free parameter, the tolerance $\varepsilon$ ($\delta$ and the grid spacing $s$ are fixed). We calibrate it to the rank-preservation target $\rho \geq \targetRho$ on the \emph{binding} network --- the sparsest, where the canonical grid model is least conservative and the schedule samples least. Among the three, that is Cary: its actual reach falls below the canonical estimate (Figure~\ref{fig:val_reach}), so it meets the target with the thinnest margin. Tuning $\varepsilon$ on Cary and applying it unchanged elsewhere therefore secures the denser networks by construction. The resulting default is $\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$, at which Cary's closeness clears the target at every distance (minimum $\rho = \caryMinRho$, at 20\,km); a looser tolerance drops it below $\targetRho$.

\subsection{Real-world validation}

Tables~\ref{tab:validation}--\ref{tab:cary_validation} report results for the three networks. All achieve $\rho > \targetRho$ for closeness and betweenness at every distance from 1--20\,km. At shorter distances the schedule prescribes $p \geq \varphi$, so the implementation computes exactly and $\rho = 1$ holds by construction; genuine estimation error appears only where sampling engages (10 and 20\,km here), and the reported margins above $\targetRho$ refer to those sampled distances. The 20\,km betweenness is the limiting case for each network: $\rho = \glaMinRhoBetweenness$ (London), $\rho = \madridMinRhoBetweenness$ (Madrid), and $\rho = \caryMinRhoBetweenness$ (Cary).

Speedup emerges only at the longer distances, where a small fraction of nodes is sampled (Figure~\ref{fig:val_speedup}). London and Madrid are dense, with actual reach at or above the canonical model (Figure~\ref{fig:val_reach}), so the schedule oversamples them and their margins are wide; Cary is sparse --- its reach lies below the canonical curve --- which is why the tolerance is calibrated against it and why its margins are the tightest of the three.

\subsection{Error structure}

Absolute errors grow with reach, but \emph{relative} errors shrink (Figure~\ref{fig:error_crossover}): the most important nodes (those with the highest centrality and largest neighbourhoods) are estimated most precisely. Errors are spatially uniform, with no systematic bias in dense cores or sparse peripheries (Figure~\ref{fig:spatial_error}). Most nodes remain in the same centrality decile under sampling, with the strongest stability in the upper deciles (Figure~\ref{fig:decile_transition}).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig2_error_vs_reach.pdf}
  \caption{Per-node median errors pooled across reach quartiles at distances where $p < 1$, for Greater London (circles), Greater Madrid (squares), and Cary (triangles). (A) Absolute error increases with reach. (B) Relative error decreases with reach: precision scales with centrality importance.}
  \label{fig:error_crossover}
\end{figure}

%==============================================================================
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
%==============================================================================

\subsection{Practical guidance}

In \cityseer{}, the user sets a single parameter ($\varepsilon$, the error tolerance) and the library automatically determines how much to sample at each distance. Algorithm~\ref{alg:deterministic} gives the full procedure for manual implementations. Table~\ref{tab:distance_lookup} and Figure~\ref{fig:guide} show the schedule at standard distances.

\input{tables/tab_distance_lookup}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig3_practical_guide.pdf}
  \caption{(A) Sampling probability $p$ vs.\ analysis distance at default settings. (B) Theoretical speedup $1/p$. These values assume no boundary buffer; on buffered networks, the implementation falls back to exact mode when $p \geq \varphi$ (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}), so sampling only engages at longer distances.}
  \label{fig:guide}
\end{figure}

On a buffered network the live fraction is $\varphi < 1$, and sampling engages only where $p < \varphi$ (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}). For example, at $\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$ the schedule prescribes $p \approx \hoeffdingPFiveKm\%$ at 5\,km, but if $\varphi \approx \glaLiveFraction$ (Greater London) exact mode is cheaper and sampling does not engage. At 10\,km ($p \approx \hoeffdingPTenKm\%$) and 20\,km ($p \approx \hoeffdingPTwentyKm\%$), sampling is active and the realised closeness speedup is $\varphi / p$ rather than $1/p$ (betweenness, which sources from every node, realises $1/p$). Larger study areas have higher $\varphi$ and benefit more; the compact Cary study area, with a low $\varphi$, sees little closeness speedup though betweenness still gains.

Halving $\varepsilon$ quadruples the number of required samples. A tighter tolerance ($\varepsilon = 0.04$) suits networks sparser than the validation set, or publication-quality work, but roughly halves the speedup. A looser tolerance ($\varepsilon = 0.08$--$0.1$) trades ranking accuracy for additional speed and is suitable for exploratory work where approximate rankings suffice.

The two metrics bind at different ends of the density range. Betweenness is noisier than closeness --- its contributions are heavier-tailed --- and is the limiting metric on the dense networks; on the sparse suburban network, closeness binds and sets the default tolerance. A closeness-only analysis on a dense network can therefore safely use a looser tolerance.

For small networks (under about 1{,}000 nodes), exact computation completes in seconds and sampling is unnecessary. For unfamiliar network types, a pilot comparison at one long distance (e.g., 10\,km) can verify that $\rho > \targetRho$ before committing to the schedule.

\subsection{What the guarantee does and does not cover}

The Hoeffding bound guarantees that absolute errors stay within a tolerance; our validation measures something different --- whether the \emph{ranking} of nodes is preserved (Spearman $\rho$) --- and no formal bound connects the two. The bound provides the mathematical \emph{form} of the schedule; the ranking accuracy is a validated empirical outcome.

Three factors make the bound loose, so that on all but the sparsest networks the schedule is markedly more conservative than necessary. First, the Hoeffding bound uses only the range of contributions and ignores the actual (much smaller) variance. Second, the union bound treats node-level errors as independent, though they are positively correlated. Third, rank preservation is more forgiving than additive error: street-network centrality spans several orders of magnitude, so small absolute errors rarely change the ordering among well-separated nodes, and the highest-centrality nodes --- those with the largest neighbourhoods --- are estimated most precisely.

\subsection{Scope and limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

The schedule applies to shortest-path (metric) distance only. Angular distance (simplest-path) \citep{Turner2007} does not satisfy the subpath optimality assumed in the betweenness derivation and remains to be tested. Validation spans dense European metros and a low-density US suburb, with the tolerance calibrated on the sparsest of these; networks within this density range are therefore covered, but genuinely rural or otherwise sparser networks may need a tighter tolerance ($\varepsilon = 0.04$) or a pilot comparison.

The canonical grid model substitutes a fixed spacing for actual network structure: denser networks are oversampled, while sparser ones fall below the canonical estimate and rely on the calibrated tolerance $\varepsilon$ to preserve rank (Figure~\ref{fig:val_reach}). Effective speedup also depends on the live fraction $\varphi$, which shrinks as the buffer grows relative to the study area, so large distance thresholds on small study areas see less benefit.

Natural extensions include validation on angular distance and a broader range of morphologies, and tighter efficiency via adaptive per-node sampling, online stopping criteria \citep{Borassi2019}, or variance-aware bounds \citep{Pellegrina2023}.

%==============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
%==============================================================================

We have presented a sampling schedule for localised network centrality that depends only on the analysis distance. The core idea is to replace the global network size in existing concentration bounds with the local catchment size (reach), and to use a fixed canonical grid model so that the schedule requires no per-network calibration of the reach estimate. The schedule has a single tolerance parameter $\varepsilon$, which we calibrate once on the sparsest validated network so that denser networks are covered by construction. The same sample serves both closeness and betweenness. Boundary buffer nodes must be included in the source pool to prevent edge effects, which reduces the effective speedup but preserves accuracy. Validation on three street networks spanning the density range --- Greater London, Greater Madrid, and the low-density suburb of Cary, NC --- at distances from 1 to 20\,km confirms that sampled rankings closely match exact rankings ($\rho \geq \overallMinRho$), with errors distributed uniformly across the network.

The schedule is implemented in the open-source \cityseer{} Python package.\footnote{\href{https://github.com/benchmark-urbanism/cityseer-api}{github.com/benchmark-urbanism/cityseer-api}} Analysis scripts and validation data are available in the repository's \texttt{analysis/sampling/} directory.

\section{Technical Details}

\paragraph{GLA network preprocessing.}

The Greater London Authority road network is sourced from Ordnance Survey Open Roads data (GeoPackage format).

Preprocessing steps:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Remove invalid and empty geometries
  \item Explode multi-part geometries
  \item Build NetworkX graph from edges
  \item Remove filler nodes (degree-2 nodes that do not represent junctions)
  \item Remove dangling nodes (dead-end segments $< 20\,$m)
  \item Consolidate nearby nodes (threshold 1\,m)
  \item Extract largest connected component
\end{enumerate}

Final network: \glaNnodes{} nodes.

\paragraph{Madrid network.}

The Greater Madrid metropolitan network (\madridNnodes{} live nodes) is sourced from the official \emph{Red Viaria} road-network dataset for the Community of Madrid and preprocessed using the same consolidation pipeline as the GLA network. As for the other networks, the boundary delimiting the live area is geocoded from OpenStreetMap via OSMnx \citep{Boeing2017}.

\paragraph{Cary network.}

The Cary, NC network (\caryNnodes{} live nodes) is built from US Census TIGER/Line \emph{edges} --- the topologically integrated road layer, which is natively noded at intersections (the cartographic \emph{roads} layer is not, and does not build a connected graph). Road edges (\texttt{ROADFLG = Y}) are loaded for every county intersecting the analysis area plus its \glaBuffer{}\,km buffer, then passed through the same consolidation pipeline as the GLA network. The live area is the Cary municipal boundary; the surrounding region supplies the buffer.

\paragraph{Correctness verification.}

We verified the Rust-based \cityseer{} implementation against NetworkX \citep{Hagberg2008} on test networks across distance thresholds from 200\,m to 3200\,m, both distance heuristics, and both metrics. The maximum per-node difference was below $10^{-6}$ in all configurations, attributable to floating-point precision.

\paragraph{Inverse-probability weighting.}
\label{sec:appendix_ht}

When only a fraction $p$ of nodes are sampled as sources, each sampled contribution is scaled by $1/p$ to estimate what the full computation would have produced. This is a standard Horvitz--Thompson estimator \citep{Horvitz1952} and is unbiased whenever $p > 0$. The source pool includes both live and buffer nodes (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}), ensuring that every node which contributes in exact mode has a chance of being sampled.

For closeness, each source's contribution to a target depends only on the distance between them, so contributions from different sources are independent. For betweenness, the Brandes decomposition likewise yields independent per-source terms, so the same argument applies.

\paragraph{Betweenness over all routes.}

Betweenness counts shortest paths from every node, live or buffer: a path between two buffer nodes that passes through the interior legitimately credits the live intermediate it traverses, so excluding it would under-count boundary nodes. The \emph{live} designation therefore filters only which nodes' values are reported, not which sources run. Each ordered pair $(s,t)$ contributes with weight $\tfrac{1}{2}$ on undirected graphs (the two orderings of a symmetric pair are counted once between them) and $1$ on directed graphs; buffer-to-buffer routes through the interior are included. Under sampling this estimand is unchanged, and the Horvitz--Thompson $1/p$ scaling applies uniformly with no per-pair correction.

\paragraph{Implementation in \cityseer{}.}

The sampling model is implemented in the \cityseer{} Python package (version 4.25+). Sampling is enabled via the \texttt{sample=True} flag. When enabled, the library automatically computes the live fraction $\varphi$ and falls back to exact mode at distances where $p \geq \varphi$ (Section~\ref{sec:buffer}). The \texttt{centrality\_shortest} function computes both closeness and betweenness from shared Dijkstra traversals in a single call:

\begin{verbatim}
from cityseer.metrics import networks

gdf = networks.centrality_shortest(
    network_structure,
    nodes_gdf,
    distances=[500,1000,2000,5000,10000,20000],
    sample=True
)
\end{verbatim}

Convenience wrappers (\texttt{closeness\_shortest}, \texttt{betweenness\_shortest}) are available for computing a single metric, but using them separately forgoes the shared-traversal advantage.

The default error tolerance ($\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$) and failure probability ($\delta = \hoeffdingDelta$) are set in \texttt{cityseer.config}. The \texttt{cityseer.sampling} module provides helper functions for custom workflows:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \texttt{compute\_distance\_p}: deterministic $p$ from distance via canonical grid model (recommended entry point)
  \item \texttt{compute\_hoeffding\_p}: Hoeffding bound from a given reach value (for experimentation with non-canonical schedules)
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Reproducibility.}

All analysis scripts and validation results are available at \href{https://github.com/benchmark-urbanism/cityseer-api/tree/master/analysis/sampling}{analysis/sampling/}. The script pipeline runs sequentially from \texttt{01\_validate\_gla.py} through \texttt{06\_figures\_spatial.py} via \texttt{run\_all.py}, with each script's outputs documented in its header.
